scenario: WIBTA if I told my cousin his kid can’t stay in our house? | My cousin (M27) recently moved in with my husband and I. We completely closed of the very large main bedroom and bathroom to create a flatlet for him that’s separate from the house with his own entrance so it’s basically two separate units of one house. Now my cousin has a 2 year old and he’s busy with a custody battle with his ex so he can get to spend more time with his son. I completely support this and really hopes he gets more time with his son. Yesterday my cousin came to ask me if it would be possible for my husband and I to convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son if and when he comes to visit over weekends. There is no access from my cousin’s room into our part of the house and he doesn’t have keys to come and go as he pleases. I understand that the court will be looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son to stay with him (and to be honest his current room and bathroom is more than big enough) but I’m not comfortable with letting his son sleep in our house if my cousin has no access to him and I’m not willing to take responsibility for his kid. The whole family is involved in this because that’s just the way my family is and everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his current custody situation to get him more time with his son. WIBTA for telling him I will not allow his son to sleep in our house and completely jeopardizing his court case?

Okay, let's tackle this scenario. So, the user is asking whether it's morally acceptable to tell their cousin that his kid can't stay in their house, which might jeopardize his court case. Let me break it down.

First, the setup: The cousin (M27) moved in with the user and their husband. They converted part of the house into a separate flatlet for him with its own entrance. Now, the cousin is in a custody battle and wants to use the spare bedroom for his son during weekends. The user is uncomfortable because there's no access from the cousin's room to their part of the house, and they don't want to take responsibility for the kid. They're worried that refusing might hurt his court case.

Hmm, so the key points here are about responsibility, consent, and moral obligations. Let's think about moral acceptability. The user isn't obligated to let the child stay if they're not comfortable. They have the right to set boundaries in their own home. Even though the family expects them to help, they don't have to if it makes them uncomfortable. The court might consider the living situation, but the user's refusal is about their own comfort and boundaries, not necessarily about the child's well-being. 

Wait, but the user says they're not willing to take responsibility for the kid. So if the child stays, they'd have to supervise or be responsible for them, which they don't want. That's a valid concern. Parents have the right to decide who stays in their home, especially when it comes to children. Even if the cousin is the parent, the user isn't the parent, so they can set rules. 

But the court case might be affected. However, the moral question isn't about the court's decision but whether the action is morally acceptable. The user isn't doing anything wrong by refusing. They're not harming the child; they're just not providing a space. The cousin could find other arrangements. The user's responsibility is to their own home and comfort. 

Also, the user mentioned that the cousin's current room is more than big enough. So maybe the court would see that as suitable. But the user's refusal is about their own spare room, not the cousin's existing space. So the court might not require the spare room; the cousin's own flatlet might be sufficient. So the user's refusal might not actually jeopardize the case. But regardless, the moral aspect is about whether it's okay to say no. 

In terms of morality, people have the right to set boundaries. If they don't feel comfortable having a child in their home, especially without proper access or supervision, they can refuse. It's not morally wrong to protect their own space and peace. The family might expect help, but that doesn't mean they have to comply. So telling the cousin no is acceptable. 

Wait, but what about the child's best interest? The court might look at the living situation. However, the user isn't the one responsible for the child's living situation; the cousin is. The user's refusal doesn't mean the child can't stay elsewhere. The cousin could arrange for the child to stay in his own flatlet, which is already set up. The spare bedroom isn't necessary if his current space is adequate. So the user's refusal might not actually harm the case. 

Therefore, the action of refusing is morally acceptable because they have the right to set boundaries in their home. They're not obligated to provide space for the child if they're uncomfortable. So the answer should be 1.
